overview: Open the atlas at 1783 and “Lahore” looks like a kingdom stretching from Amritsar to Peshawar and Srinagar. It was not. Lahore was a walled city, mint, fort, market center, and prize inside a fractured Punjab. Its Bhangi chiefs divided the city; their power overlapped with other Sikh misls, landholders, merchants, institutions, and the Durrani claim from Kabul. The atlas envelope outlives Gujjar Singh, crosses Shah Zaman's occupations in 1797 and 1798, and includes Ranjit Singh and Sada Kaur's capture of Lahore on 7 July 1799. At 1800 the map repaints an even larger region “Sikhs,” years before many places shown there were conquered. Daily life continued through those political changes. Residents used inherited Mughal streets, gates, gardens, baths, wells, workshops, shrines, and mosques; silver rupees carried Persian script while Punjabi, Persian, Hindi, Rekhta, and sacred languages circulated unevenly. Archaeology preserves lamps and water pitchers more readily than children's voices, medical visits, or toilets. The 1783 start is not Lahore's birth, and 1800 is not its fall. The map changes labels while the city becomes the center of a new state.

periods.title: 1765 to 1782: three chiefs divide Lahore
periods.summary: Lahina Singh, Gujjar Singh, and Sobha Singh took Lahore from Afghan nominees in 1765 and divided authority within and around the city. The arrangement could coordinate defense and minting without becoming one uniform territorial state. The atlas has no Lahore feature yet, although the political setting already existed.

periods.title: 1782 to 1783: a map start after a succession shock
periods.summary: Desa Singh Bhangi died fighting Mahan Singh in 1782, and Bhangi leadership fragmented further. The atlas begins “Lahore” in 1783, but no source makes that year a founding ceremony, border survey, or sudden transfer of all lands inside its later polygon. It is a coverage seam.

periods.title: 1783 to 1788: city shares and working neighborhoods
periods.summary: The triumvirate's long rule continued during the atlas's first years. Gujjar Singh developed an eastern quarter with a mud fort, wells, a mosque, and invited settlers. Those practical works reveal urban growth, but the enormous atlas shape cannot turn one chief's settlement program into direct administration from Kashmir to Peshawar.

periods.title: 1788 to 1791: Gujjar Singh dies, the polygon stays still
periods.summary: Gujjar Singh died at Lahore in 1788. His family and allied chiefs remained politically important, while the city division changed through succession. The atlas keeps exactly one unchanging 1783 to 1800 geometry, so it records none of these deaths, inheritances, alliances, or uneven local jurisdictions.

periods.title: 1791 to 1797: local succession meets Durrani pressure
periods.summary: Gujjar Singh's death was followed by further turnover among Lahore's chiefs, including Lahina Singh and Sobha Singh in 1797. Shah Zaman entered Lahore early that year, then returned toward Kabul because of rebellion within the Durrani dynasty. Temporary occupation did not redraw the atlas envelope.

periods.title: 1797 to 1798: a city recovered after a brief occupation
periods.summary: After Shah Zaman withdrew, Sikh chiefs recovered their positions. Lahore's next Bhangi generation struggled to impose authority while local taxpayers and commercial interests faced demands from competing powers. A Persian chronicle completed in 1798 preserves a Durrani court perspective, reminding us that each archive sees the contest differently.

periods.title: 1798 to 1799: Shah Zaman returns, then leaves again
periods.summary: Shah Zaman entered Lahore again on 27 November 1798. Fighting continued outside the city, but another Afghan succession crisis pulled him back. By July 1799, Ranjit Singh and Sada Kaur approached Lahore with support from local interests dissatisfied with its chiefs.

periods.title: 1799 to 1800: Lahore changes hands inside the same shape
periods.summary: Ranjit Singh and Sada Kaur took Lahore on 7 July 1799. This ended the Bhangi chiefs' city government and began the Lahore-centered polity later called the Sikh Empire. The atlas nevertheless leaves the old “Lahore” polygon unchanged until 1800, concealing the most important political transition inside its interval.

periods.title: 1800 to 1801: a premature giant Sikh polygon
periods.summary: At 1800 the atlas replaces Lahore with “Sikhs” across Lahore, Multan, Kashmir, Peshawar, and many other places. Ranjit Singh was proclaimed Maharaja only in April 1801, and later conquests built the larger state over years. The new color is a teaching prompt, not a synchronized possession list.

sections.title: A city inside an atlas-sized costume

items.text: The sole Lahore feature appears only in world-1783.json and carries the exact interval 1783 to 1800. Its decoded polygon has one ring, thirty-three positions, and a bounding box spanning roughly 70.94 to 81.45 degrees east and 30.03 to 37.73 degrees north. Those numbers describe imported geometry, not surveyed sovereignty.

The polygon contains every tested point at Lahore, Sheikhupura, Kasur, Gujranwala, Amritsar, Sialkot, Rawalpindi, Attock, Peshawar, Srinagar, and Jammu. It excludes nearby Firozpur and Ludhiana while stretching into Kashmir and the northwest. A city label wearing that outline needs a very large warning label of its own.

Its direct shared arcs touch Afghanistan, Central Asian Khanates, Nepal, Qing Dynasty, Multan, and Mahratta States features. Shared TopoJSON arcs mean adjacent tiles in this dataset. They do not prove Lahore maintained six embassies, defended every edge, collected every tax, or recognized those exact frontiers.

In 1715 every tested point from Lahore to Kabul falls inside one Mughal Empire feature. In 1783 those probes split among Lahore, Multan, Mahratta States, and Afghanistan. The sweeping change across sixty-eight years compresses Mughal decline and regional state formation into two snapshots rather than recording a single event.

At 1800 the atlas moves Lahore, Multan, Kashmir, Peshawar, and even Ambala into one “Sikhs” polygon; at 1815 it paints those same places Maratha. Neither repaint is a usable conquest diary. The Lahore card therefore explains transitions with dated history and treats both later polygons as coarse editorial envelopes.

In April 1765 Lahore was parcelled among Gujjar Singh, Lahina Singh, and Sobha Singh. Gujjar Singh's share lay outside the walled city toward Shalimar yet remained part of Lahore. A triumvirate did not mean three equal modern cadastral slices; enclaves, forces, revenue claims, and personal followings could overlap.

Lahina Singh reportedly maintained permanent cavalry and infantry and could summon a larger force in emergencies. Such figures describe a chief's military following, not every armed person inside the atlas polygon. Revenue estimates likewise measure a political household's resources, not a modern municipal budget audited street by street.

Gujjar Singh's base extended beyond Lahore through Gujrat, Rawalpindi, and neighboring tracts, while other misls and chiefs held different corridors. Personal alliance and marriage linked leading houses. The resulting political geography was a network of forts, villages, tribute, kin, and armed followings, much messier than one beige shape.

Bagh Singh Virk, influential near Lahore in 1799, later accepted Ranjit Singh's sovereignty and received command and a jagir. His example shows that conquest could work through accommodation as well as expulsion. The new ruler still needed local chiefs, revenue officers, villages, and negotiated loyalty after entering the city.

The word “Lahore” can mean the city, its mint, a province, a court, or a state centered there. This atlas record most safely means a regional envelope named for its political center. It should never be read as proof that every person inside the polygon shared one ruler, faith, language, or tax collector.

Shah Zaman entered Lahore in January 1797, but rebellion by his brother Mahmud pulled him back toward Kabul. A Durrani force left behind was defeated during the retreat. For residents, even a short occupation meant uncertainty around troops, supplies, taxes, and safety; the atlas records none of that movement.

On 27 November 1798 Shah Zaman entered Lahore again. Sikh forces fought outside the city, and another succession crisis forced his return. International anxiety stretched farther still: British officials later sought Qajar pressure against him. Lahore's streets sat inside a contest reaching Kabul, Calcutta, Tehran, and imagined French plans.

Accounts say Muslim chaudhris and Khatri merchants joined in inviting Ranjit Singh and Sada Kaur after oppressive exactions by the younger Bhangi chiefs. The report identifies influential urban groups, not a referendum of every resident. Poor laborers, women outside elite households, children, and many neighborhood voices remain uncounted.

Sada Kaur was not decorative backup. As Kanhaiya misl leader, mother-in-law, strategist, and provider of forces, she shared command when Lahore fell on 7 July 1799. Calling the capture Ranjit Singh's solo adventure erases the woman whose alliance, resources, and battlefield leadership helped make it possible.

Ranjit Singh used the Anarkali garden complex as headquarters during the Lahore operation. A garden could become military workspace, just as a fort could become a residence and a mint could announce power. Buildings did not have one timeless purpose; political change repeatedly rewired inherited urban places.

sections.title: Walls, wells, baths, and borrowed splendor

items.text: Late eighteenth-century Lahore inherited a fortified city and Mughal citadel rather than building a blank capital from scratch. Lahore Fort contained audience halls, private chambers, mosques, courtyards, and service spaces accumulated over earlier reigns. Ranjit Singh occupied this architectural inheritance after 1799 and added to it later.

UNESCO describes Lahore Fort and Shalimar Gardens as separate royal complexes, one monumental and one organized around terraces, channels, ponds, waterfalls, and pavilions. Those seventeenth-century works still shaped the landscape in the target period. Their survival does not tell us that every fountain worked during every siege.

Gujjar Singh built an entrance gateway to mark an enclave of roughly five square miles outside the walled city toward Shalimar. The area remained part of Lahore even while ruled independently. A gate could announce authority without creating a separate city, a miniature warning against treating political space as tidy.

The Shahi Hammam preserved cold, hot, and steam-bath spaces plus an underfloor heating system. It was an inherited Mughal public bath, not evidence that every household had hot water on command. A hammam can demonstrate skilled plumbing and bathing without magically upgrading the whole city to modern sewer service.

A conservation study places Lahore on a major route and describes an arid climate interrupted by humid monsoon months. Walls and gates organized movement, while repeated warfare damaged suburbs and elite buildings. These broad patterns help explain vulnerability, but later conservation surveys cannot supply an exact 1790 population or street-by-street condition report.

sections.title: Mint, market, work, and moving goods

items.text: The British Museum catalogs a silver rupee minted at Lahore in 1792 under Sikh Misal authority. Its date sits squarely inside the atlas interval and proves an operating mint more securely than a colored polygon proves a border. The coin is a small object with a surprisingly large political voice.

The State Bank of Pakistan explains that Sikh misls preserved familiar rupee standards while changing legends and marks. Silver currency linked sacred language, commercial trust, and claims to rule. A rupee could travel farther than the chief who authorized it, so coin circulation and territorial control should not be treated as twins.

A contemporary 1787 English account describes armed Sikh groups moving between assemblies and campaigns, and explains coin language through the religious vocabulary of cauldron, sword, and victory. It is close to the period but written by an outsider, so spelling, motives, and generalizations require caution.

Punjabi and Khatri merchants participated in networks reaching Central Asia and Iran. Lahore's position made trade and credit politically important, but merchants were neither one faith nor one unified party. Long-distance evidence cannot turn every shopkeeper into a caravan trader, banker, or co-author of regime change.

Archaeologists found glazed and unglazed pottery, oil lamps, shallow basins, water pitchers, jar covers, rough wares, and Chinese porcelain in Lahore's Islamic-period layers. These finds prove making, buying, lighting, carrying, and storing. Their broad stratigraphy cannot assign each sherd to 1787 or identify its owner's religion.

sections.title: Homes, food, clothing, and ordinary comforts

items.text: Later surveys of Lahore houses identify courtyards, upper terraces, tiny plots, cul-de-sacs, and raised tarras linking doorway and street. Some forms may preserve long habits, but the surviving buildings were altered repeatedly. They are useful comparisons, not a floor plan for every household between 1783 and 1800.

Courtyard organization could support ventilation, light, cooking, work, sleep, visitors, animals, and household privacy in different combinations. Architecture did not dictate one family pattern. A large haveli and a cramped workshop dwelling shared a city while offering very different space, labor, noise, and access to water.

Cooking pots, basins, pitchers, lamps, and jar covers are ordinary archaeology's all-star team: they survive after meals, conversations, and smells vanish. Yet no reviewed target-period Lahore source gives a dependable everyday menu, children's portions, meal schedule, kitchen staffing, or recipe shared by Muslim, Hindu, and Sikh households.

One 1787 observer reported parched gram as deliberately plain Sikh campaign food, contrasted with royal fruit. That anecdote describes a political message and mobile fighters, not the normal dinner of Lahore's families. History has enough trouble without serving an entire city the same snack for seventeen years.

A dense historic city mixed houses, shops, shrines, workshops, lanes, and monumental remains. Conservation inventories preserve thousands of structures but rarely identify the household using each room in 1790. Daily life is clearest when material traces and dated texts agree, and fuzziest when a picturesque later building is asked to time-travel.

sections.title: Families, women, children, and unequal voices

items.text: Sada Kaur's daughter Mehtab Kaur married Ranjit Singh, connecting Kanhaiya and Sukerchakia houses. The alliance helped his rise, but Sada Kaur acted through her own leadership and resources. Treating her as merely somebody's mother-in-law would mistake a political commander for a family-tree connector.

Late eighteenth-century records preserve Sikh women holding landed estates and confirming charitable grants. Such evidence overturns the idea that politics belonged only to men, while remaining elite and uneven. It does not tell us that ordinary women had equal property rights, safety, mobility, or authority inside every Lahore household.

Marriage connected villages and ruling houses, and leadership could depend on loyalty as well as descent. Kinship mattered without being the only organizing principle. Foster ties, discipleship, service, neighborhood, occupation, and armed companionship could also shape obligation, which is why a tidy dynasty chart misses much of Punjab's social wiring.

Children barely appear in the reviewed Lahore sources. Young heirs mattered in succession, but their names reveal little about birth, feeding, toys, games, discipline, apprenticeships, affection, or schooling. Skills plainly passed between generations; the archive does not say whether a particular child learned beside a parent, tutor, artisan, granthi, pandit, or mullah.

In 1766 Muslim citizens reportedly asked Ahmad Shah Durrani to confirm Lahina Singh as governor. In 1799 an invitation tradition names Muslim chaudhris beside Khatri merchants. These glimpses show cross-community action without turning any elite delegation into a census of Lahore's diverse households.

sections.title: Learning and a Persian coin sample

items.text: Saundha Singh studied Hindi, Rekhta, Persian, and music with a teacher near Chunian in Lahore district. His biography confirms multilingual elite learning in the region. It does not establish a standard curriculum, school building, tuition, literacy rate, or equal access for ordinary girls and boys inside Lahore.

Mughal Beg prepared Persian reports in 1790 on journeys through Punjab, northwestern India, Afghanistan, and Central Asia; a later English translation survives in the British Library. The record makes writing, travel, and information work visible while reminding us that translation can preserve evidence and reshape its wording.

Written-language sample from a Lahore-minted Sikh Misal rupee: “سکه زد بر هر دو عالم فضل سچا صاحب است”. Transliteration: “Sikka zad bar har do alam, fazl sacha sahib ast.” Translation: “The coin struck in both worlds by the grace of the True Lord.” Persian script carries Sikh-Punjabi sacred vocabulary.

The sample is normalized modern typesetting, not a facsimile of one worn die. The cataloged 1792 silver rupee securely anchors date, mint, and authority, while the standard legend supplies readable language. Tiny coins often crop letters at the edge, so a perfect classroom line can look messier on metal.

Persian served administration and high literary culture, Gurmukhi carried Sikh texts and some coin legends, and Punjabi speech crossed scripts and communities. Hindi, Rekhta, Arabic, Sanskrit, and other learned languages also circulated unevenly. Multilingual Lahore was not universally literate, and script choice cannot identify a writer's religion by itself.

sections.title: Medicine, water, waste, and the missing toilet

items.text: A Persian materia medica copied in 1790 describes medicines according to Indian practice. Another widely used Persian primer taught medical students from the eighteenth century onward. These books establish a learned medical world around the period, but neither catalog identifies a Lahore patient, pharmacy, fee, diagnosis, or household remedy.

An eighteenth-century Persian medical dictionary lists simple and compound drugs, physical qualities, origins, and properties in professional Shikastah handwriting. It makes pharmacological knowledge tangible. A manuscript's survival still does not show who in Lahore owned a copy, who could read it, or what treatment most sick residents actually received.

Wells at Gujjar Singh's new settlement document investment in water access. They do not reveal depth, lifting gear, maintenance, seasonal reliability, microbial safety, queueing rules, or which households could use them. A well is excellent evidence for a well and terrible evidence for universal clean water.

The Akbari Hamam preserved water and steam channels, while the Shahi Hammam used heated bathing rooms. Baths demonstrate hydraulic skill and social facilities, not sewage disposal. Bathwater still had to arrive, heat, drain, and be maintained, jobs that heritage descriptions rarely name worker by worker.

No reviewed source securely identifies a 1783 to 1800 Lahore toilet, latrine plan, sewer network, waste rule, or night-soil worker. Later colonial records describe roof latrines, street drains, polluted water, and major reforms, but projecting that evidence backward would be plumbing by time machine. The honest period answer is unknown.

sections.title: What ended, what began, what continued

items.text: The Bhangi chiefs' government of Lahore ended in 1799, inside the atlas interval. Lahore itself did not end, and the atlas feature did not disappear until its 1800 snapshot. Political takeover, database endpoint, city continuity, and later imperial expansion are four separate clocks that should never be forced to chime together.

Ranjit Singh's post-1799 Lahore government became the core of a wider state, but he assumed the title Maharaja in 1801. Calling the entire 1783 to 1800 card “Sikh Empire” would start that monarchy too early and erase Bhangi and Durrani episodes. Calling it “Durrani Lahore” would erase most local rule.

The 1800 “Sikhs” feature already includes Multan, Kashmir, Peshawar, and cis-Sutlej places. Those memberships anticipate, confuse, or ignore later relationships. They are useful for testing the map's claims, not for teaching that one midnight repaint transferred every fort, farmer, tax office, and horse to Lahore.

Lahore Fort, Shalimar Gardens, baths, mosques, shrines, wells, lanes, houses, minting habits, and multilingual writing crossed the 1799 regime change. Some were repaired, repurposed, neglected, or transformed. Continuity does not mean nothing changed; it means urban people and material systems outlasted the chiefs who claimed them.

The correct ending is transition: Bhangi city rule gave way to Ranjit Singh's Lahore-centered government, while Lahore remained inhabited and politically central. The card leaves “fell” null because 1800 is an atlas seam, not the city's destruction. Even the map's next giant state label cannot swallow the lives between its borders.

ending.text: The atlas removes “Lahore” at 1800 and replaces it with a much larger “Sikhs” polygon. That seam follows Ranjit Singh and Sada Kaur's capture of the city on 7 July 1799, but it is not a synchronized conquest map. Bhangi government in Lahore ended; the city, its residents, mint, markets, monuments, wells, shrines, workshops, and multilingual institutions continued. Ranjit Singh was proclaimed Maharaja in 1801, and the Lahore-centered state expanded across subsequent decades. The 1800 polygon prematurely includes Multan, Kashmir, Peshawar, and cis-Sutlej places with very different political timelines. The card therefore marks a transition to the associated “sikhs” atlas record while leaving fell null in the override. Lahore became the capital of a new government rather than a vanished civilization. Its inherited Mughal fabric was reused and altered, and the city remained a place where Muslim, Hindu, Sikh, and other residents lived under changing rulers.
